summary: US division of auticon, a technology consulting company describing itself as the largest majority-autistic company in the world, with over 75% of its workforce neurodivergent, offering software, data and QA services alongside corporate neuroinclusion training.
notes: auticon was founded by an ally in Germany in 2009; the workforce is majority autistic but company leadership is not exclusively so, hence 'mixed.' Sacramento is the registered US office address.

name: Autism in Black
summary: Organization founded by Maria Davis-Pierre providing coaching, training and community support to Black parents raising autistic children, with an annual conference and podcast addressing racial disparities in autism diagnosis and services.
notes: Founder Maria Davis-Pierre is a parent of an autistic child, not stated as autistic herself, so classified ally-led despite being explicitly Black-led. Exact HQ city approximated from founder's public South Florida base.

name: Autism Science Foundation
summary: US nonprofit that funds autism research grants and fellowships and publishes plain-language summaries of autism science for families and clinicians.

name: Autistic Self Advocacy Network
summary: National advocacy organization run by and for autistic people, founded in 2006. Works on disability policy, public education, and community organizing around autism rights in the United States.

name: Autistic Women & Nonbinary Network
summary: Peer network and resource hub for autistic women, transgender, and nonbinary people, run by and for autistic people. Provides community support, publications, and advocacy from its base in Lincoln, Nebraska.

name: Camphill Association of North America
summary: Umbrella association for a network of about 15 intentional 'life-sharing' communities across the US and Canada where people with and without intellectual/developmental disabilities live together, also running the Camphill Academy and volunteer service programs.
region: Kimberton, PA (network spans multiple US states and Canadian provinces)
notes: Network includes communities in California, Minnesota, New York, Pennsylvania, Ontario and British Columbia; no single centralized headquarters confirmed, so Kimberton (a long-established community) is used as a representative location.

name: CHADD (Children and Adults with Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder)
summary: National nonprofit headquartered in Lanham, Maryland, that runs a federally funded National Resource Center on ADHD, publishes Attention magazine, and coordinates local support chapters for people with ADHD and their families.
notes: Commonly reported elsewhere as founded in 1987 by parents of children with ADHD; not independently confirmed on the current site during this pass, so left null.

name: College Autism Network
summary: US network linking researchers, disability service staff and advocates working to improve access and outcomes for autistic students in higher education, publishing research reviews and practice guides.

name: College Internship Program (CIP)
summary: US transition programme with several campuses helping young autistic and ADHD adults build skills for college, employment and independent living through individualized coaching.

name: Creative Growth Art Center
summary: Studio and gallery in Oakland founded in 1973 where adult artists with developmental, intellectual, and physical disabilities make and sell visual art. One of the earliest organizations of its kind in the United States.
notes: Founding date is given as 1973 or 1974 in different sources; founded by educator Florence Ludins-Katz and psychologist Elias Katz.

name: Creativity Explored
summary: Creativity Explored is a San Francisco studio founded in 1983 by Florence Ludins-Katz and Elias Katz that gives adults with developmental disabilities studio access, materials, and professional support to create and sell art.
notes: Curl 200 OK. Site language is 'partners with artists with developmental disabilities'; run by professional staff, not artist-governed.

name: Daivergent
summary: US platform that matches autistic and other neurodivergent jobseekers with employers and provides online skills training and job coaching.

name: Decoding Dyslexia California
summary: California chapter of the parent-led Decoding Dyslexia grassroots network, pushing for statewide dyslexia screening, teacher training and classroom accommodations.
notes: Part of the national Decoding Dyslexia network of parent-led state chapters; site returns an intermediate redirect before resolving (curl-confirmed live).

name: Decoding Dyslexia Massachusetts
summary: Massachusetts chapter of the parent-led Decoding Dyslexia grassroots network, advocating for statewide dyslexia screening, teacher training and classroom accommodations.
notes: Part of the national Decoding Dyslexia network of parent-led state chapters.

name: Decoding Dyslexia New Jersey
summary: New Jersey chapter of the parent-led Decoding Dyslexia grassroots network, campaigning for state definitions of dyslexia, teacher training, early screening and classroom access to remediation and assistive technology.
notes: Part of the national Decoding Dyslexia network, which describes itself as 'a network of parent-led grassroots movements.'

name: DFN Project SEARCH
summary: US national transition-to-employment programme placing young adults with intellectual and developmental disabilities, including autism, in structured workplace internships leading to jobs.
notes: Partnership between the Doug Flutie Jr. Foundation and the Project SEARCH model originated at Cincinnati Children's Hospital.

name: Different Brains
summary: Fort Lauderdale, Florida nonprofit producing media on neurodiversity (podcasts including Spectrumly Speaking and ADHD Power Tools), mentoring neurodivergent young adults, and running employment-readiness programming across autism, ADHD, dyslexia and other conditions.

name: Dyspraxia Foundation USA
summary: US nonprofit based in Deerfield, Illinois, dedicated to raising awareness, educating, and supporting people with dyspraxia and their families.
notes: Registered as 'Dyspraxia USA, NFP'; leadership composition not stated on homepage.

name: Extraordinary Ventures
summary: Chapel Hill, North Carolina nonprofit founded in 2007 by families, operating a portfolio of small businesses (thrift store, laundry, event center, office solutions) to create employment for adults with autism and other developmental disabilities.
notes: Founded by families responding to gaps in adult employment for people with developmental disabilities; social-enterprise employer model rather than self-advocate-run.

name: Fiesta Educativa
summary: Los Angeles nonprofit founded in 1978, one of the first US organizations serving Latino families of children with developmental disabilities, running special-education advocacy training and family conferences in Spanish and English.
notes: Founded by the Eastern Los Angeles Regional Center; parent/family-led rather than led by disabled people themselves. Describes itself as California's largest nonprofit serving Latino families of children with special needs.

name: Fireweed Collective
summary: Peer-led network for people who identify as mad, crazy, or mentally ill, founded in 2002 as the Icarus Project and renamed in 2020. Runs peer support groups, workshops, and trainings centering disabled, Black, and queer communities.
notes: Formerly the Icarus Project; restructured and renamed in 2020 to foreground Black, disabled, immigrant, and queer/trans leadership.

name: Foundations for Divergent Minds
summary: Texas-based nonprofit founded and led by multiply neurodivergent autistic people, providing online neurodiversity education, healthcare-access programming, and violence-prevention work for autistic communities.

name: GRASP (Global and Regional Autism Spectrum Partnership)
summary: Autistic and neurodivergent-led nonprofit based in New York City, providing autism assessments, neurodivergent coaching, support groups and education, originally founded as the Global and Regional Asperger Syndrome Partnership.
notes: Site explicitly self-describes as 'an Autistic and Neurodivergent led' nonprofit; also lists a satellite address in Hilo, Hawaii. Name has evolved from the original 'Asperger Syndrome' branding.

name: Green Mountain Self-Advocates
summary: Vermont disability rights organization run by and for people with developmental disabilities, coordinating local self-advocacy groups across the state and organizing conferences, workshops and state-house testimony.

name: Hearing Voices Network USA
summary: The USA's national Hearing Voices Network, coordinating peer support groups, training and a resource directory for voice-hearers across the country.
region: Northampton, MA (approximate; site did not state a fixed HQ)
notes: Site blocked most automated requests with HTTP 429/403; a plain GET without www eventually returned HTTP 202. Region is an approximate placeholder in western Massachusetts, historically a hub of US peer/HV organising; a moderator should confirm the network's actual current base.

name: Indiana Resource Center for Autism (IRCA)
summary: University-based center at Indiana University Bloomington's Indiana Institute on Disability and Community, providing training, school support and community outreach on autism using what it describes as a neuroaffirming approach.
notes: University research/training center rather than a self-advocate-run organization; explicitly states a 'neuroaffirming approach.'

name: Intentional Peer Support (IPS)
summary: Training organization founded by peer-support pioneer Shery Mead teaching a relational, non-hierarchical model of peer support used across mental health and disability communities in North America and beyond.
notes: Site returns 403 to automated fetch (bot-filtering), confirmed live via curl headers. Location is an approximation based on founder Shery Mead's long-standing New Hampshire base; the organization now trains internationally.

name: International Dyslexia Association
summary: US-based nonprofit that certifies dyslexia specialists, sets standards for structured literacy instruction, and runs a network of branches supporting people with dyslexia and their families worldwide.

name: International OCD Foundation (IOCDF)
summary: Boston-based national nonprofit for OCD and related disorders, funding research, training clinicians, running educational conferences, and coordinating a network of local affiliate support groups across the US.
notes: Leadership composition not disclosed on site; coordinates a network of independent local affiliates including several included separately in this dataset.

name: Kansas University Center on Disabilities (KUCD)
summary: University of Kansas research and training center in Lawrence, Kansas, serving as the state's federally designated University Center for Excellence in Developmental Disabilities, combining research, training and community engagement co-developed with people with disabilities and families.
notes: Formed in 2024 by merging the KU Center on Developmental Disabilities and the Beach Center on Disabilities; part of the Life Span Institute.

name: L'Arche USA
summary: US national office of the international L'Arche federation of communities where people with and without intellectual disabilities share daily life, coordinating member communities across the country from Washington, DC.
notes: 1972 marks the first US L'Arche community (Erie, PA); the international federation was founded in France in 1964 by Jean Vanier. Christian community model in which people with intellectual disabilities are core members rather than sole governors.

name: LAND Gallery
summary: LAND Studio & Gallery is a nonprofit day-habilitation program in Brooklyn, NY, founded in 2005 by the League Education and Treatment Center, teaching life skills through art alongside professional artists.

name: Learning Disabilities Association of America (LDA)
summary: National membership organization founded in 1963, providing information, advocacy and a professional/family network on learning disabilities, headquartered near Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania.
notes: One of the oldest US learning-disability organizations; site does not disclose whether people with learning disabilities hold governance roles.

name: MindFreedom International
summary: Coalition of grassroots groups founded in 1990 by psychiatric survivors, based in Eugene, Oregon. Advocates against forced psychiatric treatment and for human rights and alternatives in mental health care.
notes: Membership is majority psychiatric survivors; site states MFI "was started by psychiatric survivors."

name: National Autism Center
summary: US research and training centre, part of the May Institute, that reviews autism intervention evidence and publishes practice guidelines used by schools and clinicians.

name: National Empowerment Center
summary: Peer-run mental health advocacy and training organization based in Lawrence, Massachusetts, founded in the early 1990s by psychiatric survivors including Judi Chamberlin and Daniel Fisher, promoting recovery and self-determination outside the traditional clinical model.
notes: Site content is heavily JS-rendered so automated fetch could not confirm all details; founding by psychiatric survivors including Judi Chamberlin and Daniel Fisher is well documented in secondary sources.

name: NeuroClastic
summary: Autistic-run nonprofit media outlet publishing essays and resources almost exclusively by autistic contributors, positioned as a counterpoint to deficit-based autism narratives and recruiting writers from underrepresented backgrounds.
region: United States (online, no fixed HQ stated)
notes: Volunteer-run, distributed nonprofit with no stated physical headquarters; site explicitly states contributors are 'almost exclusively autistic.' Coordinates are an approximate US placeholder, not a confirmed office location.

name: Neurodiversity Employment Network
summary: Philadelphia-region network connecting employers, service providers and jobseekers to build employment pathways for neurodivergent adults.

name: Neurodiversity Podcast
summary: Long-running podcast and media project hosted by a counselor specializing in gifted and neurodivergent learners, interviewing researchers, educators and neurodivergent guests on ADHD, autism, giftedness and related topics.
notes: Host location approximated from publicly known professional base; not independently confirmed via site content due to JS rendering.

name: NIAD Art Center
summary: NIAD Art Center is a nonprofit studio in Richmond, California for adult artists with developmental and physical disabilities, founded in 1982, where staff support artists in creating and selling work.
notes: www.niadart.org 301-redirects to niadart.org (final 200 OK, curl-verified). Site does not state a leadership model explicitly.

name: OCD Colorado
summary: Denver-area affiliate of the International OCD Foundation, running the annual 'One Million Steps for OCD' walk, educational presentations, and community engagement for the Colorado OCD community.
notes: Official IOCDF affiliate.

name: OCD SF Bay Area
summary: San Francisco Bay Area affiliate of the International OCD Foundation, distributing OCD information, running peer support groups, and advocating for access to affordable, appropriate treatment.
notes: Official IOCDF affiliate.

name: OCD Twin Cities
summary: Saint Paul-based nonprofit and International OCD Foundation affiliate serving the Minneapolis-Saint Paul area, running support groups and connecting people with OCD treatment providers.
notes: Official IOCDF affiliate.

name: Passion Works Studio
summary: Passion Works Studio is a nonprofit collaborative art studio in Athens, Ohio, creating paid creative work for artists with and without developmental disabilities, best known for its handmade Passion Flowers.
notes: Founding year not stated on official pages checked (site references '20 years' of undated copy and Patty Mitchell working there 'since 1994'); could not independently verify this session. 'mixed' leadership reflects the site's own framing as 'creative people with and without developmental differences' working collaboratively, plus 'we wanted to create an organization that follows the lead, talent and interests of our artists.'

name: People First of California
summary: Statewide self-advocacy organization run by and for people with intellectual and developmental disabilities under the banner 'Advocates Training Advocates,' with an all-self-advocate board coordinating local People First chapters across California.
notes: Board of directors is composed of people with intellectual/developmental disabilities.

name: People First of Washington
summary: Statewide self-advocacy organization for people with intellectual and developmental disabilities based in Olympia, Washington, running local county chapters focused on advocacy, education and peer community.
notes: Site does not explicitly state governance composition, but follows the People First self-advocacy model in which chapters are member-run by people with intellectual/developmental disabilities.

name: Project LETS
summary: Grassroots peer-support and mental-health organization founded in 2009 in Providence, Rhode Island, explicitly led by and for people with lived experience of mental illness, disability, trauma and neurodivergence, running crisis support and campus chapters.
notes: Site states it is 'led by and for folks with lived experience of mental illness/madness, Disability, trauma, & neurodivergence.'

name: Project Onward
summary: Project Onward is a nonprofit studio and gallery in Chicago, founded in 2004 out of the city's Gallery 37 youth program, providing studio space, materials, and career support to more than 60 adult artists with disabilities and mental illness.

name: Pure Vision Arts
summary: Pure Vision Arts is a studio and exhibition space in New York City, founded in 2002 as a program of The Shield Institute, staffed by art-education and art-therapy professionals who support artists with autism and other developmental disabilities.
notes: purevisionarts.org 301-redirects to www.purevisionarts.org (final 200 OK, curl-verified).

name: ReelAbilities Film Festival: New York
summary: Film festival dedicated to disability representation on and off screen, founded in 2007 at the Marlene Meyerson JCC Manhattan and now the flagship of a touring ReelAbilities network across the US.
notes: Leadership marked unknown: available sources name JCC Manhattan and co-directors but do not state whether disabled people hold leadership/staff roles.

name: Rising Tide Car Wash
summary: Florida car wash founded by the family of an autistic young man, employing a majority-autistic workforce and used as a training model shared with other family-run businesses.

name: Self Advocates Becoming Empowered (SABE)
summary: National coalition of self-advocates with intellectual and developmental disabilities, formally established in the early 1990s at the Second People First Conference in Nashville, with founding members and leadership drawn from self-advocates in every US state.
region: Ohio (national office; exact city not confirmed)
notes: Founding members Nancy Ward, Roland Johnson and Tia Nelis were themselves self-advocates with developmental disabilities. Site redirects to sabeusa.com; exact headquarters city not independently confirmed.

name: Sibling Leadership Network
summary: National nonprofit with state chapters, run by and for adult siblings of people with disabilities, providing information, support programs, advocacy training and research on the sibling experience across the lifespan.
notes: Led by siblings of people with disabilities themselves rather than by disabled people or parents; hosted at the University of Illinois Chicago's disability studies program. Exact HQ city not stated on site; Chicago used based on UIC affiliation.

name: Sins Invalid
summary: Bay Area disability justice performance project, founded around 2006, creating theatrical work centering disabled artists of color and queer disabled artists and running the Disability Justice Hothouse education series; a fiscally sponsored project of Dancers' Group.
notes: Founding year inferred from a 2026 '20th anniversary' reference on the site. Centers disabled-led performance and disability justice organizing; not autism/neurodiversity-exclusive but explicitly disability-led.

name: Stanford Neurodiversity Project
summary: Program at Stanford Medicine, recently renamed the Stanford Center for Neurodiversity and Human Potential, running education, employment, and research initiatives for autistic and other neurodivergent people.
notes: Name is in transition from "Stanford Neurodiversity Project" to "Stanford Center for Neurodiversity and Human Potential"; both names appear on Stanford's own pages.

name: Stimpunks Foundation
summary: Nonprofit founded in December 2021 and built by and for neurodivergent and disabled people, providing mutual aid, creator grants, open educational resources and consultation, with leadership including autistic and ADHD board and staff members.
notes: Site does not state a physical HQ; region approximated from founders' publicly known Texas location.

name: Superfest International Disability Film Festival
summary: Longest-running disability film festival in the world, founded in 1970, now produced by the Paul K. Longmore Institute on Disability and the San Francisco Disability Cultural Center in the Bay Area.
notes: Leadership marked unknown: sources confirm disabled people serve as judges but do not explicitly state staff/leadership disability status.

name: TASH
summary: Washington, DC-based international disability rights organization founded in 1975 (originally for people with severe/profound disabilities), doing advocacy, research and policy work with membership spanning self-advocates, families and professionals.
notes: Originally the American Association for the Education of the Severely and Profoundly Handicapped; membership explicitly includes 'people with disabilities' alongside researchers and family members, but governance details not disclosed.

name: TEACCH Autism Program
summary: Autism education and clinical training program at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill, originator of structured teaching methods used in classrooms and services worldwide.

name: The Art of Autism
summary: San Diego-based 501(c)(3) nonprofit, founded 2005, that promotes autistic artists via an online gallery, exhibits and film festivals; states its board is approximately 50% autistic.
notes: Explicitly self-reports ~50% autistic board composition on its own fact sheet; active with content through August 2026.

name: The Color of Autism Foundation
summary: Detroit-area nonprofit founded in 2009 by a parent of an autistic child, providing culturally specific autism support, training, and a support group for Black fathers and co-parents of autistic children.
notes: Registered address is in Beverly Hills, MI (metro Detroit); the organization describes its direct-service base as Detroit families.

name: The Neurodiversity Alliance (Eye to Eye)
summary: New York-based nonprofit, formerly known as Eye to Eye, founded by and for people with learning disabilities and ADHD, that runs a national school-based mentoring program pairing older and younger students who learn differently.
notes: Formerly Eye to Eye; eyetoeyenational.org now redirects to thendalliance.org. Sources vary between ~20 and ~25 years since founding, so an exact year is left null.

name: The Precisionists Inc.
summary: US IT services company that employs adults with autism and other disabilities as software testers, data analysts and process specialists for corporate clients.

name: Thinking Person's Guide to Autism
summary: Long-running collaborative media project publishing autism information and commentary from a mix of autistic self-advocates and parent writers, co-founded by writer Shannon Rosa and colleagues in the San Francisco Bay Area.
notes: Site returns 403 to automated fetch (bot-filtering), confirmed live via curl headers. Editorial team mixes autistic and non-autistic writers; region is an approximation based on a co-founder's public location, not a stated office address.

name: Tourette Association of America
summary: The main US national organization for Tourette Syndrome and tic disorders, founded in 1972, funding research, training healthcare providers and educators, and running a nationwide support-group network.
notes: Originally named the Tourette Syndrome Association; leadership composition (self-advocate vs. professional governance) not disclosed on site.

name: Ultranauts
summary: US software quality-engineering company built around a majority-autistic, fully distributed workforce, designing its own management practices around neurodivergent strengths.
notes: Co-founded by an autistic entrepreneur; company describes itself as neurodiversity-led.

name: Visionaries + Voices
summary: Nonprofit studio in Cincinnati, founded in 2003, offering visual art space, materials, and exhibition opportunities to more than 125 artists with disabilities.

name: Wildflower Alliance
summary: Peer-run Massachusetts mental health and recovery organization, formerly named the Western Massachusetts Recovery Learning Community, offering peer respite, a peer support line, and training grounded in the psychiatric survivor and Mad Pride movements.
notes: westernmassrlc.org now redirects here, confirming this is the renamed continuation of the Western Massachusetts Recovery Learning Community (rebranded 2021). Peer-run by people with lived psychiatric-survivor experience.

name: William & Mary Neurodiversity Initiative
summary: Participatory campus initiative at William & Mary in Williamsburg, Virginia, running events and programming on autism, ADHD and other brain differences, with autistic writer John Elder Robison serving as Neurodiversity Scholar-in-Residence.
notes: Working group includes administrators, faculty, staff, alumni and students alongside an autistic scholar-in-residence.

name: Wisconsin FACETS
summary: Milwaukee-based nonprofit serving as Wisconsin's family-to-family resource for children with disabilities, offering a special-education help desk, resource referrals and IEP training at no cost to families.
notes: Founded by Jan Serak; a parent/family-oriented resource center rather than a self-advocacy organization.

name: Zeno Mountain Farm
summary: Vermont-based nonprofit running free, accessible camps and film/theater projects that mix people with and without disabilities, established in 2008 on the principle that disability is not a problem to be fixed but a difference society must accommodate.
notes: Grew out of the Cheshire Project, a 2005 Venice, CA filmmaking collective, before the Vermont farm property was purchased in 2008.

name: Aletea
name_local: Aletea - Asociación civil uruguaya para el colectivo autista
summary: A Montevideo civil association of families and professionals working for the social inclusion of autistic people in Uruguay from a neurodiversity and social-model-of-disability framework, offering training, multidisciplinary support and advocacy.
notes: Family- and professional-run rather than self-advocacy-led, but explicitly adopts the neurodiversity paradigm.

name: Radio Vilardevoz / Mad Pride Uruguay
summary: A psychiatric-survivor-led community radio and cultural project born in 1997 at the Vilardebó psychiatric hospital in Montevideo, now running a cultural space and organizing Uruguay's Mad Pride marches against institutionalization and electroshock.
notes: Ran Uruguay's first Mad Pride march in Plaza Independencia, September 21, 2023; site active with posts through September 2026.

name: RUATDAH (Uruguayan ADHD Support Network)
name_local: Red Uruguaya de Apoyo al TDAH
summary: A family-led Uruguayan network created because no organization previously existed to support people with ADHD, providing information, guidance and community for families and advocating for better public policy on diagnosis and treatment.
notes: Explicitly family-run rather than adult-ADHD self-advocacy; site actively maintained with recent articles and event promotion.

name: Vietnam Autism Network (VAN)
name_local: Mạng lưới Tự kỷ Việt Nam
summary: Voluntary nonprofit network of parents, autism specialists, and autistic individuals recognised by Vietnam's Ministry of Labour, running national autism awareness activities.
notes: Governing board is elected from parent-group representatives across six provinces/cities; member of the ASEAN Autism Network.

name: Pan African Network for Persons with Psychosocial Disabilities (PANPPD)
summary: Continent-wide network, active in over 20 African countries with 50-plus partner organisations, advancing the rights and inclusion of people with psychosocial disabilities under the principle 'Nothing About Us Without Us.'
notes: HQ city inferred from a +263 (Zimbabwe) contact number on the site, not explicitly stated; the network's own member list by country was not published on the pages checked. Reports 15+ years of work and 1M+ lives impacted. Successor/relative of the older Pan African Network of Users and Survivors of Psychiatry (PANUSP).
